A condiment is a food substance that you add to other food — usually just before eating or while eating — to make it taste better, more interesting, or more suited to your preference. Condiments are not the main food itself; they are extras that sit alongside or on top of the main dish to enhance its flavor.

Think of it this way: when you eat a burger, the burger patty and the bun are the main food. But the ketchup, mustard, and mayonnaise you spread on it? Those are condiments.
What condiments actually do

Condiments serve one or more of these purposes:

  • Add flavor — Salt, soy sauce, and hot sauce make food taste sharper, saltier, or spicier.
  • Add contrast — A tangy condiment like mustard can balance a rich, fatty food.
  • Add moisture or texture — Mayonnaise or a chutney can make dry food more pleasant to eat.
  • Personalize taste — Condiments let each person adjust the food to their own liking at the table.

The key thing is that condiments are supplementary — they support and improve the main food, but they are rarely the point of the meal by themselves.
What condiments look like

Condiments come in many physical forms:

  • Liquid or pourable — ketchup, soy sauce, hot sauce, vinegar, Worcestershire sauce
  • Semi-solid or spreadable — mayonnaise, mustard, hummus, butter (when used as a spread)
  • Chunky or thick — salsa, chutney, relish, pickle
  • Dry or granular — salt, pepper, chili flakes (though these are sometimes called seasonings or spices, they are broadly condiments when used at the table)
  • Paste-like — wasabi, harissa, anchovy paste
Common examples you likely already know

Here are widely recognized condiments from around the world:

  • Ketchup / tomato sauce — paired with fries, burgers, sandwiches
  • Mustard — used with hot dogs, sandwiches, pretzels
  • Mayonnaise — spread on sandwiches and burgers; used as a dip
  • Soy sauce — drizzled on rice, noodles, sushi
  • Hot sauce / chili sauce — added to food for heat and spice
  • Vinegar — used on fish and chips, salads, or pickled foods
  • Relish — a chunky, tangy topping for hot dogs and burgers
  • Chutney — a thick, sweet-spicy sauce common in South Asian cuisine, served with meals, snacks, and bread
  • Salsa — used with tacos, chips, and Mexican food
  • Wasabi — the sharp green paste served with sushi and sashimi
  • Tartar sauce — served with fried fish
  • Pickles / pickle slices — placed inside sandwiches or served on the side
  • Salt and pepper — the most universal and basic of all condiments
When exactly is a condiment used?

Condiments are typically used in one of these situations:

  1. At the table, after cooking — You pour, spread, or spoon the condiment onto your food yourself. This is the most classic use. A bottle of ketchup sitting on a diner table is a perfect example.
  2. During final assembly — When building a sandwich or a burger, you apply condiments as you put it together, right before eating.
  3. As a dip — You dip pieces of food (fries, chips, bread, vegetables) directly into the condiment.
  4. On the side — The condiment is served in a small bowl or dish next to the main food, and you use as much or as little as you like.

Some condiments — like soy sauce or hot sauce — can also be added during cooking, but this does not stop them from being condiments. What defines them is that they are flavor enhancers and not the main food substance.
How condiments differ from similar-sounding things

Since you want to fully understand this word, here are important distinctions:

Condiment vs. Ingredient
An ingredient is something mixed into a dish while it is being cooked or prepared — like onions in a curry or eggs in a cake. A condiment is something added after or separately. That said, the boundary can blur — soy sauce added to a stir-fry during cooking is functioning as an ingredient in that moment, but the same soy sauce at the table is a condiment. The word "condiment" almost always implies the latter use.

Condiment vs. Sauce
A sauce is a liquid or semi-liquid component of a dish — it can be central to the dish (like a pasta sauce). A condiment is supplementary and optional. However, many sauces double as condiments — hot sauce, ketchup, and soy sauce are all both sauces and condiments. All condiments that are liquid can be called sauces, but not all sauces are condiments.

Condiment vs. Seasoning / Spice
Seasonings and spices (like pepper, cumin, or chili flakes) are often used in cooking, but when kept on the table for people to add themselves, they function as condiments. Salt and pepper shakers on a dining table are classic condiments.

Condiment vs. Garnish
A garnish is usually something decorative placed on food (like a sprig of parsley or a lemon wedge). A condiment is meant to be eaten and to add flavor. A lemon wedge can be both — it decorates the plate, but you squeeze it onto your food for flavor, making it a condiment in that moment.
The defining characteristics, summarized clearly

For something to be called a condiment, it generally:

  • Is food or a food substance (not a utensil or anything non-edible)
  • Is added to other food, not eaten on its own
  • Is meant to improve or adjust the flavor of that food
  • Is used in relatively small amounts compared to the main dish
  • Is optional — the meal can exist without it, but it is better (or more personalized) with it
  • Is typically ready to use — you don't need to cook a condiment before applying it (though some condiments are cooked or processed during their making)
Using the word in everyday sentences

Here are natural ways the word "condiment" appears in speech and writing:

  • "Could you bring the condiments? I need ketchup and mustard."
  • "Every table in the restaurant had a small tray of condiments."
  • "She always carries a small bottle of hot sauce — it's her favourite condiment."
  • "The dish was good, but it needed a condiment to give it more kick."
  • "Soy sauce is a staple condiment in Japanese and Chinese cuisine."
  • "The store has a whole aisle dedicated to condiments."
A note on cultural variation

Condiments vary enormously across cultures. What counts as an essential condiment in one cuisine might be completely unknown in another. Fish sauce is a standard condiment in Southeast Asian cooking. Chimichurri is essential in Argentine grilling culture. Mango pickle (aachar) is a beloved condiment across South Asian meals. This global variety reflects the word's broad reach — any culture that enhances food with added flavoring substances has condiments, even if the specific items differ.
The one-line definition to remember

A condiment is a flavoring substance — such as a sauce, paste, relish, or seasoning — that is added to food to enhance its taste, usually at the table or just before eating, and is supplementary to the main dish rather than being the main dish itself.
